problems.title: Two Sum
problems.statement: Given an array and a target, exactly one pair of distinct elements sums to the target. Output their zero-based indices in ascending order.
problems.constraints: `2≤n≤100000`, `-10^9≤ai,target≤10^9`; exactly one pair.

examples.explanation: `2+7=9`, and the indices are ascending.
The equal values at indices 0 and 1 are the unique valid pair.

problems.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
problems.statement: Choose at most one buy day followed by a later sell day. Return the maximum non-negative profit.

examples.explanation: Buy at 1 and sell at 6.
No later price is higher than an earlier price.

problems.title: Contains Duplicate
problems.statement: Report whether any value occurs at least twice.

examples.explanation: The value 1 occurs twice.
Every value occurs exactly once.

problems.title: Product of Array Except Self
problems.statement: For each position output the product of every input value except the value at that position.
problems.constraints: `2≤n≤18`, `-10≤ai≤10`; division is prohibited; results fit signed 64-bit.

examples.explanation: Each output is the product of the other three values.
Every product except the zero position includes a zero.

problems.title: Maximum Subarray
problems.statement: Output the largest sum among all non-empty contiguous subarrays.

examples.explanation: The subarray `4 -1 2 1` has the greatest sum.
The best non-empty subarray is the single value -2.

problems.title: Valid Anagram
problems.statement: Determine whether the two input strings contain exactly the same multiset of letters.
problems.input_format: Two lowercase strings `s` and `t` on one line.
problems.constraints: `1≤|s|,|t|≤100000`; both inputs contain only lowercase English letters.

examples.explanation: Both strings have identical letter counts.
Their character multisets differ.

problems.title: Valid Palindrome
problems.statement: Determine whether the lowercase string reads identically from both directions.
problems.constraints: `1≤|s|≤100000`; `s` contains only lowercase English letters.

examples.explanation: The string equals its reverse.
The first and last characters do not match symmetrically.

problems.title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
problems.statement: Output the maximum length of a contiguous substring containing no repeated character.
problems.constraints: `1≤|s|≤100000`; `s` contains only lowercase English letters.

examples.explanation: `abc` is a longest substring without repetition.
Any valid substring contains only one `b`.

problems.title: Group Anagrams
problems.statement: Group anagrams and print groups deterministically. Sort words within each group and sort groups by their first word; print each group on one line, words separated by spaces.
problems.constraints: `1≤n≤1000`; total word length is at most 100000; every word has length at least 1 and contains only lowercase English letters.

examples.input:
6
neat tea tan ate nat bat
examples.output:
ate tea
bat
nat tan
neat
examples.explanation: Words share a group exactly when their sorted-letter keys match.
All three words belong to one sorted group.

problems.title: Longest Palindromic Substring
problems.statement: Output the longest palindromic substring. If several have the same maximum length, output the one with the smallest starting index.
problems.constraints: `1≤|s|≤2000`; `s` contains only lowercase English letters.

examples.explanation: `bab` and `aba` tie, so the earliest start wins.
The longest palindrome has even length.

problems.title: Reverse Linked List
problems.statement: Reverse the serialized singly linked list and print its values.
problems.output_format: Reversed values on one line; empty input list produces an empty line.
problems.constraints: `0≤n≤100`; each list value is a signed 32-bit integer.

examples.explanation: Each next link is reversed.
Values are preserved while order reverses.

problems.title: Merge Two Sorted Lists
problems.statement: Merge two nondecreasing serialized lists and print the resulting nondecreasing list.
problems.input_format: `n m`, then list A, then list B; `0≤n,m≤100`.
problems.output_format: All merged values, or an empty line.
problems.constraints: `0≤n,m≤100`; both serialized lists are nondecreasing; each value is a signed 32-bit integer.

examples.explanation: Select the smaller current head repeatedly.
Merging with an empty list returns the other list.

problems.title: Linked List Cycle
problems.statement: The serialized list has values followed by a cycle entry index. `-1` means the tail points to null; otherwise the tail points to that index. Output whether a cycle exists.
problems.constraints: `0≤n≤100`; `-1≤entry<n`; values are signed 32-bit integers; `-1` means the tail points to null.

examples.explanation: The tail points back to index 1.
The tail points to null.

problems.title: Remove Nth Node From End
problems.statement: Remove the `n`th node counted from the tail. The input always has `1≤n≤length`; print the remaining list.
problems.output_format: Remaining values, or an empty line.
problems.constraints: `1≤length≤100`; `1≤n≤length`; each value is a signed 32-bit integer.

examples.explanation: The second node from the tail is removed.
The tail is removed.

problems.title: Add Two Numbers
problems.statement: Each list stores one non-negative integer in reverse digit order. Add the two numbers and print the result in reverse digit order.
problems.input_format: `n m`, then `n` digits and `m` digits; `1≤n,m≤100`, digits 0–9.
problems.output_format: Result digits, least significant first; omit leading zeroes except that zero is printed as `0`.
problems.constraints: `1≤n,m≤100`; every list value is a decimal digit `0..9`; each list is reverse-digit order.

examples.explanation: The represented numbers are 342 and 465, totaling 807.
99+1=100, represented least-significant digit first.

problems.title: Valid Parentheses
problems.statement: Determine whether every bracket in the string is correctly opened, nested, and closed. Alphabet is `()[]{}` only.
problems.constraints: `1≤length≤100000`; every character is one of `()[]{}`; the input is non-empty.

examples.explanation: Every opening delimiter closes in the correct order.
The closing bracket does not match the opening bracket.

problems.title: Min Stack
problems.statement: Process operations on an initially empty stack. `push x`, `pop`, `top`, and `min` are given; queries are valid. Print one answer per `top` or `min` operation.
problems.constraints: `1≤q≤100000`; `push` values satisfy `-10^9≤x≤10^9`; every `pop`, `top`, and `min` operates on a non-empty stack.

examples.input:
6
push 3
push 1
min
pop
top
min
examples.explanation: The minimum changes when the value 1 is removed.
Both queries observe the only stack value.

problems.title: Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation
problems.statement: Evaluate an integer expression in reverse Polish notation. Tokens are integers or `+ - * /`; division truncates toward zero. The expression is valid and has no division by zero.
problems.constraints: `1≤n≤1000`; tokens are integers or `+ - * /`; the expression is valid, leaves one result, and never divides by zero; intermediate results fit signed 64-bit.

examples.explanation: `(2+1)*3=9` in postfix order.
`13/5` truncates toward zero before adding 4.

problems.title: Daily Temperatures
problems.statement: For each temperature, output the number of days until a warmer temperature; output 0 if none exists.

examples.explanation: Each value reports the wait for its next warmer day.
Every day waits exactly one day except the last.

problems.title: Sliding Window Maximum
problems.statement: Output the maximum value in every contiguous window of width k.
problems.constraints: `1≤k≤n≤100000`; every array value is a signed 32-bit integer.

examples.explanation: The deque keeps the maximum candidate for each width-three window.
A width-one window contains its only element.

problems.title: Climbing Stairs
problems.statement: Count ways to reach stair n when each move climbs one or two stairs. The order of moves matters.
problems.constraints: `1≤n≤45`; each move advances exactly one or two stairs.

examples.explanation: The two sequences are 1+1 and 2.
The recurrence counts all one-step/two-step sequences.

problems.title: House Robber
problems.statement: Houses in a line contain non-negative amounts. Rob no two adjacent houses; output the maximum amount.
problems.constraints: `1≤n≤100000`; `0≤amount[i]≤10000` for every house.

examples.explanation: Rob houses 0 and 2.
Rob houses containing 2, 9, and 1.

problems.title: Coin Change
problems.statement: Given coin denominations and a target amount, output the fewest coins needed, or -1 if impossible. Each denomination may be reused.
problems.input_format: `m amount`, then m positive coin values; `1≤m≤20`, `1≤amount≤10000`.
problems.constraints: `1≤m≤20`; `1≤amount≤10000`; every coin denomination is a positive integer; coins may be reused.

examples.explanation: No combination of 2 and 4 makes 3.

problems.title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
problems.statement: Output the length of a strictly increasing subsequence.
problems.constraints: `1≤n≤100000`; `-10^9≤ai≤10^9`; increasing means strictly increasing by index.

examples.explanation: One LIS is 2,3,7,101.
One LIS is 0,1,2,3.

problems.title: Word Break
problems.statement: Given a string and a dictionary, determine whether the string can be split into one or more dictionary words. Words may be reused.
problems.input_format: String `s`, then integer m, then m lowercase dictionary words; `1≤|s|≤100`, `1≤m≤50`, word lengths≤20.
problems.constraints: `1≤|s|≤100`; `1≤m≤50`; dictionary words have length `1..20`; all characters are lowercase English letters; words may be reused.

examples.explanation: The string splits as leet + code.
